title: The complex exponential and logarithm
objectives: Work with the complex exponential and the many values of the logarithm.

screens.prose: Solve $e^z = -2$. For real $x$, $e^x > 0$, so there is no real answer. Write $z = x + iy$: then $e^z = e^x e^{iy}$, so we need $e^x = 2$ and $e^{iy} = -1$. Drag $z$ until the caption reads $f(z) = -2$.
screens.question: Which $z$ with $0 \le \operatorname{Im} z < 2\pi$ solves $e^z = -2$?

hints.text: The size of $e^z$ is $e^x$; its direction is $y$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Choose $x$ to fix the size and $y$ to fix the direction.

byKey.no-angle: $e^{\ln 2} = 2$, not $-2$. The minus sign needs $e^{iy} = -1$, so $y = \pi$.
byKey.half: $e^{i\pi/2} = i$ points up. To point at $-2$ you need half a turn, $y = \pi$.

explain.text: $e^x = 2$ gives $x = \ln 2 \approx 0.6931$, and $e^{iy} = -1$ gives $y = \pi$. Adding any multiple of $2\pi$ to $y$ also works, so every $\ln 2 + i(\pi + 2\pi k)$ is a solution, for whole $k$.

screens.prose: $e^z = e^x(\cos y + i\sin y)$. Horizontal lines go to rays from 0, vertical lines to circles. Drag $z$ straight up and watch its image.
screens.question: How far up must $z$ move before $e^z$ returns to the same point?

options.why: After $\pi$ the image is on the other side: $e^{z + i\pi} = -e^z$.
Moving up by 1 turns the image by 1 radian, not a full turn.
Moving up only turns the image. A full turn of $2\pi$ brings it back.

hints.text: Moving up by $t$ turns the image by $t$ radians.

feedback.correct: $e^{z + 2\pi i} = e^z e^{2\pi i} = e^z$: $e^z$ has period $2\pi i$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Drag up and stop where the image is back where it started.

explain.text: Moving $z$ up by $t$ multiplies $e^z$ by $e^{it}$, a turn of $t$ radians. So $e^z$ repeats with period $2\pi i$, and the grid wraps once round per $2\pi$ of height. It is never 0, since $|e^z| = e^x > 0$.

screens.prose: So the **complex exponential** $e^z = e^x(\cos y + i\sin y)$ has modulus $e^x$ and argument $y$. It has period $2\pi i$ and is never 0. Evaluate one value.
screens.question: Write $e^{1 + i\pi/3}$ as $p + qi$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Split $e^{1 + i\pi/3} = e^1 \cdot e^{i\pi/3}$.

byKey.added: You kept the parts of the exponent as the parts of the answer. Use $e^x(\cos y + i\sin y)$.
byKey.swapped: You swapped cosine and sine: the real part is $e\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{e}{2}$.
byKey.no-e: You dropped the factor $e^1 = e$ from the real part of the exponent.

explain.text: $e^{1 + i\pi/3} = e\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{e}{2} + \frac{e\sqrt3}{2}i \approx 1.3591 + 2.3541i$. Its modulus is $e$ and its argument $\pi/3$.

screens.prose: Undoing $e^z$ gives the **logarithm** $\log z = \ln|z| + i\arg z$, with infinitely many values, $2\pi i$ apart. The **principal logarithm** $\operatorname{Log} z = \ln|z| + i\operatorname{Arg} z$ takes $\operatorname{Arg}$ in $(-\pi, \pi]$. The map shows $\operatorname{Log}$.
screens.question: What is $\operatorname{Log}(1 + i)$?

hints.text: Drag $z$ to $1 + i$ and read the caption.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take $\ln$ of the modulus and $i$ times the principal argument.

byKey.no-ln: You used the modulus itself. The real part is $\ln|z| = \ln\sqrt2$.
byKey.mod-squared: You used $\ln|z|^2$. The modulus is $\sqrt2$, so the real part is $\ln\sqrt2 = \frac12\ln 2$.
byKey.degrees: The argument goes in radians: 45 degrees is $\pi/4$.

explain.text: $|1 + i| = \sqrt2$ and $\operatorname{Arg}(1 + i) = \frac{\pi}{4}$, so $\operatorname{Log}(1 + i) = \ln\sqrt2 + \frac{\pi}{4}i \approx 0.3466 + 0.7854i$. Check: $e^{0.3466} = 1.4142$ at angle $\pi/4$.

screens.prose: Complex powers are defined by $z^w = e^{w\log z}$. Since $\log i = i\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k\right)$, the power $i^i$ has a value for each whole $k$. The table gives two; the principal value uses $k = 0$.
screens.question: What is the principal value of $i^i$?

feedback.correct: $i^i = e^{i \cdot i\pi/2} = e^{-\pi/2} \approx 0.2079$, a real number.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $e^{i\operatorname{Log} i}$ with $\operatorname{Log} i = i\frac{\pi}{2}$.

byKey.sign: You used $e^{+\pi/2}$. The exponent is $i \cdot i\frac{\pi}{2} = -\frac{\pi}{2}$.
byKey.times: $-1$ is $i \times i$. A power needs $e^{w\log z}$.

explain.text: $i\operatorname{Log} i = i \cdot \frac{i\pi}{2} = -\frac{\pi}{2}$, so $i^i = e^{-\pi/2} \approx 0.2079$. The other values are $e^{-\pi/2 - 2\pi k}$: 0.000388 at $k = 1$ and 111.3178 at $k = -1$. All of them are real.

screens.prose: $\operatorname{Arg}$ jumps from $\pi$ to $-\pi$ across the negative real axis, the **branch cut** of $\operatorname{Log}$. $\operatorname{Log}(-1 + 0.001i) \approx 0.0000005 + 3.1406i$. Drag $z$ from just above the negative real axis to just below it. Curves on the map break at the cut.
screens.question: What is the imaginary part of $\operatorname{Log}(-1 - 0.001i)$?

hints.text: Below the axis the principal argument is negative.

feedback.correct: Just below the cut $\operatorname{Arg}$ is near $-\pi$: $\operatorname{Log}(-1 - 0.001i) \approx 0.0000005 - 3.1406i$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Below the negative real axis the principal argument is close to $-\pi$.

byKey.above: That is the value just above the cut. Below it the argument is near $-\pi$.
byKey.pi: $\pi$ is the argument on the cut itself, at $-1$. Just below it is about $-3.1406$.

explain.text: A step of 0.002 across the cut changes the imaginary part from $3.1406$ to $-3.1406$, a jump of almost $2\pi$. The real part, $\ln|z|$, does not jump. So $\operatorname{Log}$ is analytic everywhere except on the cut and at 0.

screens.prose: For positive reals, $\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b$. Try the same rule for $\operatorname{Log}$ with $z = w = -1$.
screens.question: Is $\operatorname{Log}((-1)(-1)) = \operatorname{Log}(-1) + \operatorname{Log}(-1)$?

options.text: No: the left is $\operatorname{Log} 1 = 0$, the right is $2\pi i$

options.why: $\operatorname{Log} 1 = 0$, because $\operatorname{Arg} 1 = 0$. Only the right side is $2\pi i$.
$\operatorname{Log}(-1) = i\pi$, so the right side is $2\pi i$, not 0.

feedback.correct: $0 \ne 2\pi i$: the rule holds for $\operatorname{Log}$ only up to a multiple of $2\pi i$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $\operatorname{Log} 1$ and $\operatorname{Log}(-1)$ separately.

byKey.b: You assumed the rule and added. $\operatorname{Log} 1 = \ln 1 + i \cdot 0 = 0$.

explain.text: $\operatorname{Log} 1 = 0$, but $\operatorname{Log}(-1) + \operatorname{Log}(-1) = 2\pi i$. Adding arguments can leave $(-\pi, \pi]$, and $\operatorname{Log}$ then brings the answer back by $2\pi i$. So $\operatorname{Log}(zw) = \operatorname{Log} z + \operatorname{Log} w$ holds only up to a multiple of $2\pi i$.

screens.prose: Write `principal_log(z)` from `math.log` and `math.atan2`, without `cmath.log`. $\operatorname{Log} 0$ is undefined, so raise `ValueError` for 0. The starter uses $\arctan(b/a)$, the quadrant trap from level 1.
screens.question: Fix `principal_log`.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests, two of them in the left half plane and one at 0. Results are compared with `cmath.isclose` (relative 1e-9, or the absolute tolerance shown).

feedback.correct: `atan2` gives $\pi$ for $-1$ and $-3.1406$ just below the cut.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is $-1$: `atan(0 / -1)` is 0, but the arrow points left, so $\operatorname{Arg} = \pi$. Use `atan2`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is $i$: `z.real` is 0, so `atan(b / a)` divides by zero. `atan2(1, 0)` is $\pi/2$.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 is $z = 0$: raise `ValueError` before taking the log.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. `math.atan2(z.imag, z.real)` takes the imaginary part first.

explain.text: `math.atan2(y, x)` returns the principal argument in $(-\pi, \pi]$, apart from a signed zero, and `math.log(abs(z))` the real part. The result matches `cmath.log` everywhere but at 0, where both refuse.

screens.prose: Along a path that circles 0, the principal values jump by $2\pi i$ at the cut. `continuous_log(zs)` takes a list of points and adds a multiple of $2\pi i$ to each $\operatorname{Log}$. Then the imaginary part never jumps by more than $\pi$ between neighbours.
screens.question: Complete `continuous_log`.

widget.starter:
import cmath
import math


def continuous_log(zs):
    # start from the principal value, then add multiples of 2*pi*i
    return [cmath.log(z) for z in zs]

tests.call: continuous_log([cmath.exp(1j * k * math.pi / 2) for k in range(9)])
continuous_log([cmath.exp(-1j * k * math.pi / 2) for k in range(9)])[-1]

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests. They cover two turns each way, one turn, a path that avoids the cut and an empty list. Lists are compared point by point within absolute 1e-12.

hints.text: If the jump from the last value is above $\pi$, subtract $2\pi i$; below $-\pi$, add it.
Use `while`, since a jump may need more than one shift.

feedback.correct: Twice round the circle ends at $4\pi i \approx 12.5664i$; the principal values go $0, \frac{\pi}{2}, \pi, -\frac{\pi}{2}, 0, \dots$
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 goes twice round, so the last value is $4\pi i$. After each point, compare with the previous one and shift by $2\pi i$.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 goes clockwise: subtract when the jump is above $\pi$ and add when it is below $-\pi$.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Compare with `out[-1]` only once `out` has an entry.

explain.text: Each principal value is right up to a multiple of $2\pi i$. We pick the multiple that keeps the path continuous, so twice round climbs to $4\pi i$. A pricing library tracks the branch of a logarithm this way.

screens.prose: The Heston model's characteristic function contains $e^{c\log G(u)}$ with a non-whole-number $c$. Along the pricing integral, $G(u)$ circles 0 several times at long maturities. The chart shows the imaginary part of $\log G$ along such a circle. The principal branch jumps; the continuous one does not.
screens.question: What do the jumps do to a price computed by integrating $\varphi$?

options.text: They make $\varphi$ jump and the price wrong. Fix: track the branch, or avoid the cut
Nothing, because $e^{\operatorname{Log} G}$ does not depend on the branch
options.why: True for $e^{\log G}$ itself. But $e^{c(\log G + 2\pi i)} = e^{c\log G}e^{2\pi ic}$, and $e^{2\pi ic} \ne 1$ unless $c$ is whole.
The path winds round 0 more at long maturities, so the trap bites there.

options.text: They are rounding noise and average out
options.why: Each jump is $2\pi$ in the imaginary part, not noise. It shifts $\varphi$ by the factor $e^{2\pi ic}$.

hints.text: So $\varphi$ jumps at each crossing; track the branch.

feedback.correct: Each crossing multiplies $\varphi$ by $e^{\pm 2\pi ic} \ne 1$: the integrand jumps and the price is wrong.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What happens to $e^{c\log G}$ when $\log G$ jumps by $2\pi i$?

byKey.b: You treated $c$ as 1. With a non-whole $c$, the branch changes the value of $e^{c\log G}$.

explain.text: Each crossing of the cut multiplies $\varphi$ by $e^{\pm 2\pi ic}$: the little Heston trap (Albrecher, Mayer, Schoutens and Tistaert, 2007). The fixes are a formula whose $G$ never crosses the cut, or tracking the branch as `continuous_log` does. A log return $\ln(S_T/S_0)$ never meets the cut, because prices are positive.

ideas: $e^z = e^x(\cos y + i\sin y)$ has modulus $e^x$ and argument $y$; it has period $2\pi i$ and is never 0.
$\log z = \ln|z| + i\arg z$ has infinitely many values $2\pi i$ apart; $\operatorname{Log} z$ takes $\operatorname{Arg} z$ in $(-\pi, \pi]$.
$\operatorname{Log}$ jumps by $2\pi i$ across the negative real axis, so $\operatorname{Log}(zw) = \operatorname{Log} z + \operatorname{Log} w$ only up to $2\pi i$; powers are $z^w = e^{w\log z}$.

formula.name: The principal logarithm
formula.note: Undefined at 0; every other value of $\log z$ adds $2\pi ik$.

byKey.neg: $-\pi$ is outside $(-\pi, \pi]$. The principal argument of $-1$ is $+\pi$.
byKey.zero: $\ln 1 = 0$ is only the real part. The argument adds $i\pi$.

explain.text: $\operatorname{Log}(-1) = \ln|-1| + i\operatorname{Arg}(-1) = 0 + i\pi$. This is $e^{i\pi} = -1$ read backwards.

byKey.ln-one: You used $|i| = 1$ as the real part. The real part is $\ln 1 = 0$.

explain.text: $|i| = 1$ gives real part $\ln 1 = 0$, and $\operatorname{Arg} i = \pi/2$. So $\operatorname{Log} i = i\pi/2 \approx 1.5708i$.

feedback.correct: $|e^z| = e^x > 0$, so $e^z$ is never 0; $\operatorname{Log} 0$ is undefined.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What is the modulus of $e^z$?

explain.text: $|e^{x + iy}| = e^x$, which is positive for every $x$. So $e^z$ takes every value except 0, and $\operatorname{Log} 0$ is undefined.

options.text: Python computes $e^{\operatorname{Log}(-8)/3}$, the principal cube root

options.why: The answer is far from $-2$: it is a different root, $2e^{i\pi/3}$.
$(-2)^3 = -8$, so it does. Python picks another root.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A fractional power uses the principal logarithm.

explain.text: $(-8)^{1/3} = e^{\frac13\operatorname{Log}(-8)} = e^{\frac13(\ln 8 + i\pi)} = 2e^{i\pi/3} = 1 + 1.7321i$. It is one of the three cube roots from level 1; $-2$ is another.
